A diva is either a supremely celebrated female performer — or a person who is outrageously demanding and difficult because they believe they are extraordinarily special.

Those two meanings sound very different, but they are deeply connected. Here is the full picture.

In its purest sense, a diva is a world-class female performer — most traditionally, a great opera singer. Not just a good one. A legendary one. Someone whose voice, talent, and stage presence are so extraordinary that she stands in a category above other performers. Maria Callas, for example, is considered one of the greatest divas in opera history.

The word carries enormous respect and admiration in this sense. Calling someone a diva is saying: this person is gifted at a level most people never reach. She has mastered her craft, she commands a stage, and audiences adore her.

Over time, the word spread beyond opera. In popular music, film, and entertainment broadly, a diva came to mean any enormously successful, celebrated, and commanding female performer. Whitney Houston, Mariah Carey, Céline Dion, Beyoncé — these artists are called divas as a compliment. It means they are icons. They have extraordinary talent, a larger-than-life presence, and a devoted following. There is a glamour and a grandeur to them that sets them apart.

So in this sense: diva = a brilliant, celebrated, iconic female performer.

Here is where it gets interesting. Because these celebrated performers were so famous and so talented, many of them also developed a reputation for being extremely difficult to deal with. They would make enormous demands — a specific temperature in the dressing room, certain foods that must be present, staff who must not make eye contact, hours of special preparation. They could be temperamental, explosive, and convinced that normal rules did not apply to them.

Over time, people began using "diva" to describe this behavior — the demanding, high-maintenance, entitled attitude — even when talking about someone who is not a famous performer at all.

So today, if someone calls a person a diva in everyday conversation, they usually mean:

  • This person is excessively demanding and expects special treatment.
  • They overreact to small inconveniences, throwing tantrums or making scenes.
  • They act as if they are more important than everyone around them.
  • They are high-maintenance: a lot of effort, attention, and accommodation must go into keeping them happy.
  • They have a strong sense of entitlement — a belief that they deserve to be catered to.

For example: a colleague who refuses to work unless the office temperature is exactly to their liking, complains loudly to the manager over tiny issues, and expects everyone to adjust their plans around them might be called a diva. A friend who turns every minor inconvenience into a dramatic crisis, and who always needs to be the center of attention, might be called a diva.

In this sense: diva = a person who is self-important, demanding, difficult, and high-maintenance.

What makes "diva" such a rich word is that it often lives between admiration and criticism at the same time.

When people call a famous star a diva, they might mean both things at once: yes, she is impossibly demanding and exhausting to work with — but she is also breathtakingly talented, and somehow the two things feel connected. There is a strange admiration for the sheer scale of the personality. A diva does not apologize for having enormous standards, enormous expectations, and an enormous sense of her own worth.

This is why calling someone a diva can feel like a backhanded compliment — or a fond insult, depending on the situation. Among friends, "oh, she's such a diva" might be said with laughter and affection. In a workplace, it might be said with exhaustion and frustration.
Who Can Be Called a Diva?

Originally, the word was used only for women. And it still carries a strongly feminine connotation — part of what the word evokes is a glamorous, dramatic, larger-than-life female personality.

However, in modern usage, especially in informal speech and in LGBTQ+ communities (where the word is often used with great warmth and celebration), "diva" can be applied to men or to anyone. A man who is outrageously dramatic, demanding, and self-important might also be called a diva.

The word has two layers — talent/greatness on one side, demanding/difficult behavior on the other — and in real usage, these two layers often overlap.

At the high end: a diva is an icon, a legend, an extraordinary performer who commands the world's admiration.

At the everyday end: a diva is someone who acts like an extraordinary, world-commanding legend — whether or not they actually are one.

The humor and the sting of calling an ordinary person a diva comes precisely from that gap: they are behaving like they are Maria Callas, but they are just someone arguing with a waiter about the temperature of their soup.
